title: Permission Set Groups and muting
summary: Predict effective permissions when a permission set group mutes a grant that is also supplied elsewhere.
prerequisites: M01: an access matrix with restricted users.
Junior permission sets and field-level security.
learningObjectives: Explain the scope of a muting permission set.
Trace a permission through multiple assignment paths.
Verify dependent permissions and group recalculation.

sections.heading: Understand the mechanism
body: A permission set is a reusable bundle of grants. A permission set group combines several bundles for a working persona, such as Northstar sales coordinator. Muting adjusts permissions contributed by that particular group. It does not place a universal deny on the user, and it does not rewrite the original permission set that another group may reuse.

Imagine a VIN Maintenance permission set that grants Edit on Vehicle__c.VIN__c. The Data Steward group needs the grant. The Sales Coordinator group also includes this reusable permission set but mutes VIN editing. A user receiving only the coordinator group should not gain that edit permission through it. If the same user also receives VIN Maintenance directly, the independent grant remains.

Evaluate effective permissions by drawing paths rather than looking at a single checkbox. Profile grants, direct permission sets, and other permission set groups can each contribute access. After applying muting within its own group, combine the remaining grants. Muting a supporting permission can affect permissions dependent on it inside the group, so read the dependency information instead of treating every checkbox as independent.

Changes to a permission set group require recalculation. Testing a group while its calculated state is not current can produce misleading observations. Record the group's status and test the actual field operation after the update has completed. A disabled field in one page layout is weaker evidence than an operation using the real effective field permissions.

callouts.text: Muting changes one path of permission contribution, not the final user into a denied state.

sections.heading: Northstar Motors worked example
body: Anna receives Sales Coordinator, whose muting permission set removes VIN Edit. Max receives Data Steward. Anna should read a visible vehicle's VIN without editing it; Max may edit the synthetic VIN if the remaining object and record permissions permit it. Now assign VIN Maintenance directly to Anna. Predict her edit access before testing. It returns because a different assignment path supplies it.

Remove the direct assignment and add a second group granting the same field permission. The result should again demonstrate an independent path. Keep record access constant throughout these experiments: changing both sharing and FLS would make the cause ambiguous.

callouts.text: If Anna still edits VIN after muting, name every possible independent source before changing the mute.

sections.heading: Build and inspect
body: Use existing Vehicle__c.VIN__c, a synthetic vehicle visible to both personas, and a restricted user. No new object or field is needed.

steps.title: Build the reusable permission
steps.instruction: Create VIN Maintenance with the object and field grants needed for the experiment. Add it to two groups and mute VIN Edit only in Sales Coordinator.
steps.expected: The underlying permission set remains unchanged.

steps.title: Test four assignments
steps.instruction: Compare coordinator only; coordinator plus direct permission set; coordinator plus Data Steward; and coordinator after both independent grants are removed. Wait for current group calculation.
steps.expected: The four observations follow the contribution paths.

steps.title: Inspect dependency effects
steps.instruction: In a separate reversible experiment, examine what happens when a prerequisite permission is muted. Read the configuration's dependent-permission information, then restore the original group.
steps.expected: You can explain any dependent change instead of calling it random behavior.

sections.heading: Failure cases and boundaries
body: A profile or unrelated permission set may already grant the field permission. Start from a minimal persona and inventory assignments. Otherwise, all four configurations may appear identical even though muting works correctly.
Do not use a destructive operation on customer records to prove a permission. VIN editing can be tested on a synthetic record, followed by restoration of its original value.

callouts.text: A muted permission in one group cannot revoke the same grant received from another source.

exercise.title: Explain a permission that survived muting
exercise.brief: Submit the four-path experiment with a small diagram and observed results.
steps: Apply the smallest correction that meets Anna's requirement without breaking Max's role.
acceptance: The explanation distinguishes group-local muting from effective user permissions.
All four assignment combinations are considered.
Group recalculation and unchanged record access are recorded.
exercise.stretch: Explain one limitation and propose a small follow-up experiment before extending the implementation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Does muting alter the reused permission set?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. It limits the permissions contributed through its associated group.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can a direct assignment restore access?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It supplies the grant independently of the muted group.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should be checked before blaming a group?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The user's full assignment inventory, profile grants, the group calculation state, and whether object and record access are held constant.

recap: Wait for recalculation before comparing results.
Use minimal changes that preserve other personas.
